Evita is a nineteen seventy-eight musical by composer Andrew Lloyd Webber and lyricist Tim Rice that chronicles the rise of Eva Perón from illegitimate poverty to First Lady of Argentina and a beloved icon who died of cancer at age thirty-three. The show transformed musical theater by combining operatic ambition with pop-rock idioms and complex character development, announcing both composers as major voices in Broadway's future. Evita won the Tony Award for Best Musical and secured Lloyd Webber's reputation as the defining Broadway composer of the late twentieth century.

The musical is based loosely on the life of Eva Perón, who lived from nineteen nineteen to nineteen fifty-two. She married Argentine president Juan Perón and became a charismatic voice for the working poor before her early death. The musical premiered in London in nineteen seventy-eight before transferring to Broadway. Interestingly, it opened simultaneously with a major commercial film adaptation in nineteen ninety-six starring Madonna, which significantly widened its cultural reach.

The musical reframes Eva's ambition and seduction as political performance. She climbs to power using charm, sexuality, and manipulation as tools rather than through naive ascent. This reframing was central to the show's sophistication.

One of the musical's most iconic moments is the anthem Don't Cry for Me, Argentina. This defiant declaration is sung from a presidential balcony and has become one of musical theater's most recognizable numbers. Lloyd Webber's score moves between lavish operatic passages, tango rhythms, and contemporary rock idioms, reflecting Argentina's cultural hybridity and Eva's refusal to fit a single mold.

The production includes a Che Guevara character, who unlike the historical figure, serves as narrator and moral antagonist, critiquing Eva's mythology and self-aggrandizement throughout the work.

The musical sparked a major film adaptation in nineteen ninety-six that solidified its place in global pop culture and introduced its songs to audiences who had never seen the stage show. Tim Rice brought narrative sophistication and social critique to musical theater through this collaboration. The work also showcases how musical theater could tackle serious biographical and political subjects. Cats is another Lloyd Webber hit that helped define nineteen eighties Broadway's musical aesthetics, while The Phantom of the Opera was Lloyd Webber's subsequent major success, building on lessons learned from Evita. The musical's connection to Argentina, the historical and geographical foundation of Eva Perón's story, remains central to its political context.
